Testing times 
 
The LME backwardation which flared out following a record one-day warrant cancellation has largely 
unwound following deliveries into LME warehouses in Asia, mostly due to exports from China.  In the 
USA, the withdrawals of LME material have slowed, as have those from Comex warehouses. 
 
Demand for refined copper in China and Europe remains subdued, while in the USA it appears to be 
holding up relatively well.  On the other hand, refined production growth continues to be modest. This 
is leaving the spot market to react to shifts in the availability of exchange and Chinese bonded stocks. 
 
The price has come under pressure due to the combination of the unwinding of the backwardation and 
the potential for Greece to leave the Eurozone and, more recently, the threat of Spanish banks opening 
another chapter in the saga of the single currency.

Backwardation on LME unwinding… 
The cash copper price on the LME fell by over $800/t 
between 3rd May and 31st May, slipping below 
US$7,500/t on the morning of the 31st to its lowest level 
since 5th January.  The price decline was due to the 
latest developments in the Eurozone crisis, with Greece 
likely to leave the euro and, more recently, fears that 
troubles at Spanish banks could open a new and more 
dangerous chapter in the single currency’s saga. 
In addition, the latest slide in the price followed the 
widest backwardation (cash to 3-m) on the LME since 
just before the global financial crisis started.  The 
backwardation had resulted from a short covering rally 
in the wake of the largest ever one-day cancellation of 
warrants on the LME.  Those short on the LME were 
caught out by the sudden reduction in available stock in 
the LME system and had to bid up nearby prices to 
cover their positions.  The average cash-to-3 month backwardation in the second half of May narrowed to 
around $40/t from just over $100/t in the first half of the month as more metal was delivered into LME 
warehouses.  At the time of writing the back had narrowed to almost nothing.  The market rumours were 
that the cancellation was the work of one large trader who was squeezing short positions held mainly by 
Chinese smelters, several of which made an announcement that they would make a concerted effort to 
deliver metal to the LME to help rebalance the market. 
…due mainly to Chinese exports of surplus cathode… 
In addition to the efforts of the Chinese smelters, over the past month we have been told by most market 
participants that there has been an increase in exports from China from bonded warehouses.  The volume 
of metal in these warehouses fell from a high of approximately 650,000t in mid-May to around 615,000t 
at the end of the month.  This is in response to the backwardation on the LME, holders of stock in China 
can export it and benefit from selling at the higher LME price, but also because of the backwardation they 
can benefit from lending the metal to the LME market (sell for cash price and simultaneously buy it back 
at the lower 3-month price) if they will require it later. 
Refined exports rose slightly to 27,420t in April, from 26,537t in March and up massively from only 700t 
in February.  Chinese market participants believe that exports in May will be 20,000t higher, which looks 
plausible given the marked increase in LME Asia warehouse stocks.  Open tonnage (total tonnage less 
material for which the warrant has been cancelled) in Asian warehouses has risen by over 37,000t so far 
in May.  We believe that the official Chinese exports for May will report a total refined import figure well

above 30,000t.  Most of the rise, which has more than tripled the level of open tonnage in the region from 
the 16,400t recorded on 3rd May, has been in the South Korean warehouses that are nearest to China. 
…with Chinese refined imports and production down… 
In China, the physical market is beginning to rebalance 
following the large rise in stocks that reached a peak last 
month.  In part this was the result of reduced imports.  In 
April, Chinese refined imports amounted to only 
272,903t, down from 345,667t in March, and we 
anticipate that May imports will fall further, possibly 
below the 200,000t level that is the monthly average 
required to make up the difference between Chinese 
domestic refined production and consumption.  The 
opposite movements in Chinese import and export levels 
resulted in a 130,000t reduction in net imports in April 
compared to February.  Scrap imports also fell, though 
less dramatically, to 370,919t gross weight in April from 
430,076t in March. 
The reduction in net imports has resulted, as already noted 
above, in a lowering of bonded warehouse stocks.  In 
addition, cathode inventory drawdowns in SHFE warehouses accelerated throughout May, falling by over 
17,000t in the first two weeks of the month and by almost 30,000t in H2, taking stocks down to 157,489t.  
The decline over the latter half of the month was the highest two-week decrease since May last year. 
…narrowing the SHFE/LME arbitrage 
As the price fell below RMB57,000/t on SHFE, mainly in response to the lower LME price but also to the 
weak domestic demand picture, the backwardation between the 3-month price and the cash-month price 
widened to average over RMB600/t over the past two weeks. This compares to an average differential of 
just under RMB100/t in the preceding period, as the increased exports to feed the LME squeeze saw 
increased demand for nearby metal in China.  The firmer SHFE price and weaker LME price has 
narrowed the arbitrage between the two exchanges to less than $100/t from over $500/t at its recent 
widest point at the end of April.  However, this narrowing is not yet translating into much of an increase 
in the premium on imported cathode in China, which remains at a low level of around $50/t. 
LME/Comex arbitrage widens 
In addition to the narrowing of the SHFE/LME negative arbitrage, the positive arbitrage between the 
LME and Comex has widened to an average of 3.5¢/lb in May (up to the 29th) from 2.7¢/lb in April and

an average negative arbitrage of 1.7¢/lb in Q1 2012.  
The move back into a positive arbitrage comes after the 
high level of cancelled warrants that started in 
December 2011 in LME warehouses in the USA.  This 
produced queues for metal to be delivered out and 
prompted traders to switch to secure metal from Comex 
warehouses, thus bidding up the Comex price relative 
to the LME.  The switch back to a positive 
LME/Comex arbitrage indicates that this process has 
run its course.  The traders have taken over 14,000t of 
copper out of Comex in May and over 27,000t since 
25th January on a cumulative basis.  The rate of decline 
has slowed to only 340t/d in the week 22nd to 29th May 
from 897t/d in the preceding three week period back to 
the beginning of May. 
This physical scarcity of metal compared to demand in 
the USA has translated into higher cathode premia.  
The premium for LME grade A delivered East Coast has risen by a cent to 6.5-7.5¢/lb.  Consumption has 
improved somewhat due to seasonally higher end-use activity.  However, the main reason for the rise in 
premia has been tighter supply, which was exacerbated by the maintenance closure of Rio Tinto’s 
Kennecott smelter-refinery in Utah for 24 days, beginning 30th April. 
European consumption outlook worsens 
The stock movements in LME warehouses have had similar though less extreme effects on premia in 
Europe.  The politically troubled Eurozone continues to suffer from poor sentiment.  In addition, this is 
translating into poor demand at semis plants, which are seeing a slower than usual seasonal uptick in 
consumption of copper.  We now forecast that Q2 refined consumption in Western Europe will be up 
1.5% y-o-y.  However, this result is only “strong” because of comparison to a weaker than usual Q2 in 
2011.  While demand is down, supply is also tight.  Regional production is expected to rise by only 4,000t 
on Q1 to 484,000t.  In addition, the mass cancellation of warrants on 20th April hit Europe, taking 19,150t 
out of the warehouses between 19th April and 28th May, which more than halved LME tonnage in the 
region to just 18,025t.  As a result, the tighter supply and weaker demand are offsetting one another and 
premia for physical metal have remained elevated at around $75-100/t. 
Mine disruptions continue 
Following updates of most global mine production, we have slightly raised refined copper output for 2011 
by 96,000t, mainly in H2.  Our refined estimate for Q1 2011 has been maintained at output of 4.7Mt, and

a slight increase in our Q2 forecast to 4.84Mt, as the small gains in some regions outweigh the lower 
forecast in others. 
We have maintained a relatively high disruption allowance for mine production in Q2, as there have been 
a string of incidents across the world.  These included protests in Peru over Xstrata’s Tintaya mine and 
Antapaccay project.  There were also a couple of short strikes among the contract workers at Escondida 
and workers at Kazakhmys’Annensky underground copper mine in Kazakhstan.  Finally, there was a two- 
day shut down at Collahuasi following the death of a worker in a drilling accident.  
The concerns about future demand for commodities generally due to the uncertain macroeconomic 
outlook, increased project costs and the tempering of the recovery in prices has also prompted some 
rethinking of projects, at least at BHP Billiton.  The company has until the end of 2012 to start the 
expansion at Olympic Dam or lose the permission to do so.  In addition to Olympic Dam, BHP Billiton is 
considering a port expansion in Western Australia for iron ore and a potash project in Canada.  Given 
changes in the economics of the various projects the company now has to decide which to go ahead with, 
as it does not have the capability to develop all three at once. 
Price likely to rebound from recent lows 
Investors have turned bearish on copper as the Greek crisis is supplanted in the headlines by fears over a 
potential Spanish banking crisis.  This is illustrated in the chart at the right which shows the Comex non-
financial investors moving steadily into a net short position.  If a financial tsunami is triggered by the 
Eurozone crisis, copper prices will be under extreme pressure from fund selling, though this is not our 
base case yet.  Having said that, the threat of a return to global economic meltdown may finally 
concentrates the minds of European politicians to solve the contradictions (principally the lack of fiscal 
union and measures such as euro bonds) at the heart of 
the euro.  Further bearish news comes from indications in 
recent press reports that China will focus stimulus efforts 
on investment rather than monetary policy means that the 
lags in this approach will not impact copper demand until 
later in the year and the H2 rebound may be more muted 
than we had been expecting. 
However, the modest reported stock level of 2.5 weeks 
of consumption means copper fundamentals are 
somewhat supportive of the price and will give pause to 
the bears to aggressively short copper.  At the time of 
writing the next downside support level of $7,445/t is 
being threatened, with $7,160/t the next one after that.  
Barring a financial meltdown, we expect the price to find 
support at $7,000/t and trade in a $7,100-8,100/t range.

Consumption trends 
Short Q1 sees tube output decline, alloy RBS steadier 
Following our observations of an uncertain start to the 
year for copper semis output, the available Q1 data for 
copper tube and alloy RBS production show mixed 
results.  Copper tube production was down 
significantly in most regions compared to Q1 2011, 
but alloy RBS output increased slightly y-o-y as North 
American and Asian production grew. Overall, we 
estimate that global copper tube produced and 
consumed in Q1 2012 decreased by4.8% y-o-y to just 
over 600,000t, mainly as a result of lower Chinese 
production.  Meanwhile alloy RBS consumption is 
believed to have increased slightly by 0.9% to just less 
than 730,000t.  We do, however, note that the quarter 
was one week shorter than the equivalent period last 
year, which did contribute to some of the production 
and consumption decreases.  
Amongst the bright spots in the quarter for copper tube consumption was the news that domestic shipments of 
Japanese air-conditioning units increased by 12% in March, compared to a year earlier, as the country 
continues its recovery and reconstruction efforts in the wake of last year’s natural disaster.  This followed a 
slower start to the year as bad weather and economic fears had reduced air-conditioning demand, helping to 
drive a 14.5% y-o-y reduction in January’s copper tube consumption.  Meanwhile Taiwan and other parts of 
Asia also saw increased copper tube consumption in 
Q1, both m-o-m and y-o-y.   
China and South Korea, however, both experienced 
declines in Q1 copper tube output, as material stocks 
that had begun to build last year were not draw down 
as expected following the Chinese New Year festival.

quarterly global uptick, and while this was mainly due 
to seasonal patterns in construction activity, there were

numbers in northern Europe have been improving mildly this year, and some of the activity that was delayed in 
H2 2011 due to alarm over the unfolding debt crisis could no longer be postponed and work has now begun.     
However, output for the quarter was down y-o-y in both copper tube and alloy RBS segments, with producers 
expressing doubtful sentiments.  Wieland-Werke AG, the German fabricator of brass mill products, stated in 
March that demand in 2012 had begun weakly, and KME Group of Italy was markedly dour in its Q1 report, 
stating that “the downward sales trend that characterized the second half of 2011 is continuing and projections 
provide no indication of an upturn throughout the first half of 2012.”  
New home-appliance subsidies to boost China demand  
Chinese copper tube production was down 3.4% y-o-y in Q1, due to reduced demand from the manufacture of 
white goods, and the shorter quarter.  It appears that there had been a build-up in stocks of certain home 
appliances in 2011, and these were not drawn down as expected after the Chinese New Year festival, as 
demand and general economic growth turned out to be more sluggish than most had been expecting.  National 
Bureau of Statistics data for Q1 2012 show that the production of freezers and washing machines in China 
was down between January and April this year compared to the same period last year, although the production 
of other goods such as air-conditioning units was up. However, air-conditioning demand has clearly fallen, as 
inventories have increased from a previous record of 11.94M units at the end of 2011, to around 25M units by 
mid-March, according to China Household Electrical Appliances Association. 
We mainly attribute the weaker demand for these 
specific products to the end of two distinct white goods 
subsidies in December 2011.  The government’s policy 
of subsidies for white goods being purchased in rural 
areas expired on 1st December (having been 
originally introduced in early 2009 in response to 
the global financial crisis) and the scrappage scheme 
for home appliances also came to an end on 31st 
December.  
However, this year’s slowing economic growth has not 
gone unremarked by the authorities.  While the 
Chinese government has ruled out introducing a 
stimulus package along the same lines as the one 
deployed in late 2008 at the height of the crisis, it is 
considering a number of measures aimed at boosting 
the economy in response to weaker than expected indicators.  On 16th May, it was announced that the 
government will introduce a number of new subsidies for energy-efficient products, including RMB26.5B to 
subsidise the purchase of energy-efficient home appliances.  These include air-conditioners, flat panel TVs, 
refrigerators, washing machines and water heaters, and are expected to directly benefit copper consumption in 
China.  The impact may not be felt until later in 2012 or even next year, however, due to the time it will take to

It was reported in March that the value of output at Canghuan Copper Products Co. Ltd. grew by 32% 
y-o-y to reach RMB2.9B in 2011. This represents growth of 32% y-o-y. The company, which is owned 
by the Golden Dragon Group, produces high precision tubes for air conditioning, oxygen-free copper 
tubes for the solar power sector, as well as microelectronic components and radio-frequency cables. In 
January, Canghuan Copper began an expansion project which will increase its production capacity from 
5,000t/y to 100,000t/y, indicating that the market for high-end precision copper products may be more 
positive than that of more basic semi-fabricated copper products. 
Q1 alloy RBS production was up slightly y-o-y in China, but down q-o-q in line with typical seasonal patterns. 
The market appears to be steadier than copper tube at present, and China remains a net importer in this segment 
which makes it more difficult for an oversupply to occur domestically.  
US awaits construction rebound 
Output in the US in the first quarter was mixed, with copper tube production down 12.5% y-o-y but alloy RBS 
output up 3.2% y-o-y to round 62,000t.   
Mueller Industries Inc. reported an annual decrease in net sales for the first quarter, from US$688M in Q1 
2011 to US$578M in the same period this year.  The company attributed around half of the decline to the 
quarter being a week shorter than last year’s Q1, and the other half to lower copper prices “which are passed on 
to customers in reduced selling prices”.  Unlike the more wary statements from European companies that we 
have reported above, Mueller takes a more cautiously optimistic view in its 2012 outlook.  The US-based 
copper tube and fittings manufacturer sees a recovery in the construction market, noting that building 
permits for US single family homes and apartments 
were up 30% in March y-o-y.  The firm believes that 
given today’s relatively low house prices and more 
affordable mortgages, the construction recovery is 
imminent, and it states it is ready to increase output 
to meet demand whenever this happens.  
Looking in more detail at the figures for US housing, 
we agree that the indicators are more positive.  The 
accompanying chart clearly shows a higher level of 
new building permits and starts in the first months of 
2012 than a year ago.  New permits in the period 
January-April are up 26.7% y-o-y, while new housing 
starts are up 24.0% during the same time frame.  
Completion numbers lag behind due to the building 
time lag, but show a positive trend in 2012 so far.

Industry News 
Consumption 
 
The China Non-ferrous Metals Fabrication Industrial Association (CNFA) announced that it 
is considering legislative changes that could see more stringent standards for introducing new 
copper processing facilities in China.  The association warned that there could be a copper 
products surplus in 2015 following the start-up of new projects, adding that processing capacity 
should not exceed production by more than 15%.  CNFA figures indicate that China produced 
10.28Mt of copper products in 2011, up by 18% y-o-y.  Processing capacity and utilisation rates 
were estimated at 12Mt/y and 90% at the end of 2011. 
 
Sindicel, an association for the Brazilian non-ferrous metals consumption industry, released 
figures indicating that Brazil’s semi-fabricated copper product output was down by 2.6% y-o-y, 
amounting to 396,900t (copper content) in 2011.  Wirerod production in 2011 was up by 1.2% y-
o-y, whereas brass mill output was down by 10.2% y-o-y.  Capacity increases in both the 
wirerod and brass mill product sectors resulted in utilisation rates falling to 47% and 66%, 
respectively, in 2011. 
 
China’s Hengyuan Copper, based in Shandong province, has begun commercial production 
from a newly installed 20,000t/y copper pipe line.  The company invested RMB380M in the line 
and expects to invest a further RMB581M to initially add a 10,000t/y copper wire line and then a 
170,000t/y low oxygen copper rod and bar line.  The project is expected for completion by the 
end of 2014.  
 
China’s Xingye Copper International Group plans to commission its 25,000t/y copper plate 
and strip project in Zhejiang province by 2014.  The company already operates a copper and 
copper alloy plate and strip plant. 
 
Aurubis AG reported that its copper products output reached 327,000t in Q1 2012, down by 
14.5% y-o-y.  Production of wirerod reached 179,000t, down by 17% y-o-y, attributed to slow 
European power grid investment.  In contrast, copper shapes and flat rolled products markets are 
expected to show robust growth in the coming quarters due to support from the US electronics 
and electrical, engine cooling and distribution sectors.  However, Aurubis does not expect a 
pick-up in the Asian market until around Q4 2012, adding that demand in Europe will most 
likely have improved by then. 
 
According to preliminary data from the Japan Copper and Brass Association, Japan’s April 
shipments of rolled copper declined by 8.1% y-o-y, to 64,914t. The fall in production was 
attributed to poor demand from the electronics sector, despite robust consumption by the 
automotive industry.  Nevertheless, shipments of rolled copper increased 3.2% m-o-m.

Mine Production 
 
On 28th May, the government of President Ollanta Humala in Peru was forced to suspend 
freedom of assembly rights in order to break up protests and roadblocks surrounding Xstrata’s 
Tintaya mine and Antapaccay project.  Protesters are campaigning against alleged 
environmental pollution from the mine and are demanding that Xstrata’s pays the local 
government a greater share of its profits.  During the week-long protest, two people were killed 
and around 50 were injured.  Xstrata reported that operations are proceeding as normal, with 
good stocks of concentrate at its port ready for shipment.  Production is currently being phased 
out at the 120,000t/y Tintaya copper mine, with the neighbouring 160,000t/y copper-in-
concentrate Antapaccay project set to commence production in August 2012. 
 
According to senior officials in the Indonesian government, a 20% duty tax on exports of metal 
ores will apply in the region from 6th May.  The move aims to encourage investment in ore 
processing facilities which would add value to exports and boost domestic industry.  Companies 
which hold Contracts of Work (COW) agreements, including Freeport-McMoRan, Vale and 
Newmont will be exempt from this new regulation; however, the government has expressed 
interest in renegotiating the COW agreements. 
 
On 25th May, Diego Hernandez, the CEO of Chile’s mining company Codelco, announced his 
resignation after taking on the role in 2010.  He will be replaced by Thomas Keller, the current 
CFO of the company.  According to company sources, Hernandez’s departure was linked to 
differences with Codelco’s board and is unrelated to the ongoing dispute over Codelco’s alleged 
option to acquire 49% of Anglo American Sur.  State-owned Codelco is the world’s largest 
copper mining company, having produced in excess of 1.8Mt of contained copper in 2011. 
 
On 23rd May, it was reported that Codelco and Anglo American had agreed to begin out-of-
court talks and suspend their respective litigation proceedings over the long-standing dispute 
over Codelco’s claim to a 49% share of Anglo American’s Chilean subsidiary Anglo American 
Sur (AAS).  The two companies have been locked in a continuing fierce legal battle since last 
October when Codelco announced its intention to exercise its option to acquire a stake in AAS.  
The break in legal proceedings is set to last until 22nd June. 
 
On 22nd May, commodities trader Glencore announced that it has increased its indirect equity 
interest in the Mutanda copper mine in the DR Congo to 60% in deals worth US$480M.  The 
company paid US$340M for a further 24.49% stake in Samref Overseas, the majority holding 
company of the mine, increasing its overall ownership in the company to 74.9%, as well as a 
further 1% stake in another holding company, Samref Congo.  The shares were purchased from 
High Grade Minerals (HGM) and Groupe Branzo, although their ownership details remain 
undisclosed.  Glencore also paid off US$140M of outstanding shareholder debts.  The 
acquisition of Mutada is part of the company’s long term plan to merge the mine with the nearby 
Kansuki project, which would cumulatively produce 160,000t/y of contained copper.  Glencore

Operations temporarily ceased at Anglo American’s and Xstrata’s jointly owned Collahuasi

Contract workers at the BHP Billiton-operated Escondida mine staged a 2-day protest over a 
bonus pay dispute, which ended on 3rd May.  Contract workers partially blocked access roads to 
the mine during the protest; however, production remained undisrupted according to an official 
statement. According to the contract workers’ union at Escondida, the mine operator is currently 
reviewing the protesters’ demands. 
 
300 copper miners at Kazakhmys’ Annensky underground copper mine in Kazakhstan ended a 
3-day strike on 6th May.  The workers were promised wage rises and no sanctions for taking part 
in the protest.  No production loss was incurred.  
Exploration and Development 
 
The board of directors of First Quantum Minerals has approved the construction of the 
Sentinel copper project in Zambia after agreeing an electricity tariff level with Zambia’s state-
owned electricity supplier, Zesco, on mutually agreeable terms.  An NI 43-101 technical report 
on the Sentinel project, released by GQM on 9th May, stated that talks with Zesco “confirm that 
power costs will actually be $0.075kWh”. Just prior to this, First Quantum announced that it 
would refuse to begin construction of the project unless a power agreement was reached.  Upon 
commissioning, the Sentinel Project will commence production at a rate of 150,000t/y of copper-
in-concentrate, before gradually increasing output to 300,000t/y or more. 
 
On May 8th, it was announced that the regional environmental commission in the Chile’s 
Patagonian region of Aysen has approved the construction of the 640 MW Cuervo 
hydroelectric plant.  The power plant is part of the US$3.6B Energia Austral project, a joint-
venture between Xstrata and energy retailer Origin Energy, which includes the construction of 
three power plants (Cuervo, Blanco and Condor) and a transmission lines.  The approval came 
amid some public concern over the project’s environmental impact.  Similar concerns have been 
voiced over several other planned hydroelectric plants in the region.  In particular, the US$3B, 
2,750MW HydroAysen project has faced fierce local opposition that has delayed construction 
for a year.  Estimates suggest that Chile needs to double its current power generation capacity of 
17,000MW to keep up with the rising consumption driven by high growth rates in the economy.

project is expected to be completed in early 2013.

On 7th May, Imperial Metals announced that its Red Chris copper-gold project in British 
Columbia was granted a mining permit.  The project has already received provincial and federal 
environmental permits between 2005 and 2006.  The mine project is expected to be 
commissioned in 2014 and will boast a copper-in-concentrate production capacity of 33,000t/y 
over a 28-year mine life.

 Rio Tinto Kennecott’s smelter-refinery in Utah has been shut down for 24 days, beginning 30th

take advantage of the mining of higher grade ore at the Bingham Canyon mine, which will result 
in higher deliveries of concentrate to the smelter in H2 2012. In 2011, the smelter-refinery
